locator.text: Display 72.3, p. 72, in the proof of Proposition 6.6

evidence: paper: \langle a_{\gamma,m} e^{ikm\Phi_\gamma}\rangle_\theta = 0 \quad (m \neq 0), \qquad f^{\circ} = f - \langle f\rangle_Y \ \text{for an angular mean } f.

provenance.note: machine audit: worker, gate, reviewer; not confirmed by a human

verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. Both halves are present, but as two declarations in two files rather than as one display. (i) The vanishing ⟨a_{γ,m}e^{ikmΦ_γ}⟩_θ = 0 for m ≠ 0 is stated directly by `HarmonicResidual.angularMean_nonconstant` (HarmonicResidual.lean:545), for the coefficient family `nonconstant c = c.erase 0`, i.e. coefficients carrying only harmonics m ≠ 0 (`nonconstant_support`, :567); it is Lean-general, covering any family of nonzero harmonics at once, where the paper writes the single harmonic m. Its proof at :548-549 is the one-line specialisation of `angularMean_field`, whose right side `c 0 x` is 0 once 0 ∉ c.support; `angularMean_const_character` with j = m*kp (nonzero because kp ≠ 0 and m ≠ 0) gives the same value for a literal single harmonic. No mathematics is added in either instantiation. (ii) The notation f° = f - ⟨f⟩_Y of (3.9) is realised by `nonbarPart`, whose body subtracts the normalized unit-square (2-torus) Haar average taken at a fixed value of the slow parameter, with the companion clause ⟨f°⟩_Y = 0 of (3.9) supplied by `nonbarPart_zeroMean` (for smooth f, and in the general version for smooth periodic f; the paper states it without a regularity hypothesis). The repository has this in two places with identical bodies `f z - mean f z.1`: the `FourierAlias` instance is over one slow real coordinate (`State = ℝ × Plane`, FourierAlias.lean:426, zero-mean lemma :437), and `SmoothFamilyTorusInverse.nonbarPart` (:963) is the general-parameter version, on `Point P = P × Plane` for an arbitrary normed space P (`abbrev Point` :20, `def mean` :33, zero-mean lemma :1007), so the slow variable is not restricted to one real coordinate. Both are stated for an arbitrary f rather than specifically for an angular mean, which is a strengthening rather than a restriction.
